chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Sound, as defined in the lecture, is which kind of wave?
why: A speaker vibrates back and forth, compressing and expanding air, producing a longitudinal pressure wave.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Why is there no sound in outer space?
choices: There is no air to compress
The frequency there is too high
Space is too cold for waves
why: Sound is molecules of air being compressed and expanded; without air there is no sound.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Bending of a sound wave around an obstacle is called:
why: Reflection = bouncing, refraction = change of angle entering a denser medium, diffraction = bending around an obstacle.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A transducer used to detect sound converts:
why: Sound is measured as pressure at a point, using a transducer to convert pressure to voltage levels.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Which is NOT one of the three major components of a multimedia system?
why: The three components are content creation, compression/storage, and delivery/distribution.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Which is NOT listed as an advantage of digital over analog?
why: Digital has many advantages, but quantization always introduces error.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Typical audio sampling rates range from:
why: Audio is sampled at 8-48 kHz; 20 Hz-20 kHz is the hearing range.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Human hearing extends from about:
why: The ear hears about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; above that is ultrasound.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Analog-to-digital conversion consists of:
why: Two main processes: sampling and quantization.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Converting a digital signal back to analog is called:
why: The reverse process (D/A) is known as interpolation.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A signal has frequency 250 Hz. Its period is:

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A 1 kHz tone travels at 340 m/s. Its wavelength is:

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A signal that does not change at all has frequency:
why: No change = zero frequency; an instantaneous change = infinite frequency.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: If the sampling period T is reduced, then:
why: Reducing T (raising f) increases the number of samples and the storage requirement.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A signal range R = 8 V quantized with 4 bits has step size:

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Going from 3 bits to 5 bits changes the step size Δ by a factor of:
why: Δ = R/2^b; two more bits divide Δ by 2^2 = 4.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: At least how many bits are needed for 1000 quantization levels?

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Quantization always introduces error because:
choices: The sampling rate is set too low
why: Each sample is represented by a finite number of bits, so the quantized value differs from the actual value.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Per the slides, music must be quantized with ___ bits and speech with ___ bits.
why: Audio for music needs 16 bits; speech requires only 8.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Uniform quantization works best when:
choices: The signal is mostly very loud
why: Uniform intervals spread the error evenly when all values in the range are equally likely; otherwise use non-linear (log) scales.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Bit rate equals:
why: Bits/second = (samples/second) × (bits/sample).

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Speech sampled at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample has a bit rate of:
why: 8000 × 8 = 64 000 bit/s (professor's table).

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Mono CD audio (44.1 kHz, 16 bits) has a bit rate of about:
why: 44 100 × 16 = 705 600 bit/s; stereo doubles it to 1.4 Mbps.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Stereo CD audio (44.1 kHz, 16 bits) has a bit rate of about:

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: AM radio at 11 kHz and 8 bits per sample produces:

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A 10-second mono clip at 8 kHz, 8 bits takes how many bytes?

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Any LTI system is fully characterised by its:
why: The output is the input convolved with the impulse response.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: In the time domain, the output of an LTI system is:
choices: Input multiplied by its own transfer function
Input sampled at the Nyquist rate
why: Time-domain view: output = input * impulse response (convolution).

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Convolution f*g integrates f multiplied by g that has been:
why: Convolution = integral of the first signal multiplied with the other signal reversed and shifted.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: The Dirac delta function is zero everywhere except x = 0, and its integral is:
why: A sharp peak bounding unit area: infinite at x = 0, integral 1.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: The sampling theorem was established by ___ and formalised by ___ in 1950.
why: Henry Nyquist (late 1920s), formalised by Claude Shannon in 1950.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A signal's maximum frequency is 10 kHz. It must be sampled at more than:
why: f_s > 2 × f_max = 20 kHz, the Nyquist sampling frequency (professor's example).

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Speech band-limited to 4 kHz needs a sampling rate above:
why: 2 × 4 kHz = 8 kHz, matching the 8 kHz telephone rate.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A signal contains 2 kHz, 5 kHz and 7.5 kHz. Its Nyquist sampling frequency is:
why: Only the highest component matters: 2 × 7.5 kHz = 15 kHz.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Sampling well above the Nyquist frequency causes:
why: Oversampling reproduces the signal correctly but creates extra storage and transmission overhead.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: Aliasing is:
choices: Random noise added by analog circuits
why: Aliasing describes loss of information when sampling below the Nyquist frequency.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: A 9 kHz tone sampled at 8 kHz is heard as:
why: |9 - 8| = 1 kHz, below f_s/2 = 4 kHz.

chapter: L2 · Sound, Sampling & Aliasing
q: The wagon wheel turning backwards in western films is an example of:
why: The movie camera has undersampled the wheels' motion in time.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: SNR is the ratio of:
why: The ratio of the power of the correct signal to the noise; a measure of signal quality.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: V_signal is 10 times V_noise. The SNR is:
why: 20 × log10(10) = 20 dB (the professor's example).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: V_signal = 5 V and V_noise = 0.05 V. The SNR is:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Signal power is 1000 times noise power. The SNR is:
why: For power use 10·log10: 10 × 3 = 30 dB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Why does SNR use 20·log10 for voltages?
choices: Power is proportional to V squared
Noise always has two equal components
why: Power ∝ V², so 10·log10(V²) = 20·log10(V).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Quantization noise is the difference between the analog value and:
choices: The noise measured on the analog line
why: Defined against the nearest quantization interval value at the sampling instant.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Quantization error is at most:
why: At most, the error can be as much as half of the interval.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The SQNR formula for a sinusoidal input is:
why: SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB, N = bits per sample.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The slide's maximum SQNR for 16-bit audio is about:
why: 6.02 × 16 = 96.3 dB; each bit adds about 6 dB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Using 6.02N, the SQNR of 8-bit audio is about:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Using 6.02N + 1.76, the SQNR of 16-bit audio is:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Going from 12 to 16 bits per sample improves SQNR by about:
why: 4 extra bits × 6.02 dB = 24.08 dB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Minimum bits for SQNR ≥ 75 dB using 6.02N:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76, the symbol N is:
why: Here N is bits. On L2 slide 29, N = 2^b means levels; do not mix them.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: For speech, the frequencies typically retained are:
why: Speech 50 Hz-10 kHz; music about 20 Hz-20 kHz.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The filter screening out both low and high frequencies at the encoder is a:
why: A bandpass (band-limiting) filter screens out lower and higher frequencies.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Which filter is applied after the DAC at the decoder?
why: High frequencies reappear through sampling and quantization, so a low-pass filter with the encoder's high cutoff is used.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Compared with mono, stereo audio needs:
why: Stereo information doubles the bitrate needed.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In computer networking, 'bandwidth' means:
choices: A data rate in bits per second
The number of quantization bits used
why: For analog devices bandwidth is in Hz; in networking it is the data rate in bps.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Table 6.2 lists CD audio as 176.4 kB/s. In kbps that is:
why: kB/s are bytes: 176.4 × 8 = 1411.2 kbps = 44.1 kHz × 16 × 2.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: How many bytes does one minute of CD-quality stereo audio take?
why: 1 411 200 bit/s × 60 s ÷ 8 = 10 584 000 bytes, the slide's 'about 10 MB'.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The two approaches to handling stored sampled audio are:
why: FM (frequency modulation) and Wave Table (Wave) sound.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: MIDI files are very small because MIDI:
why: MIDI is a scripting language: it codes events such as pitch, volume and instrument.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Per the slide, 3 minutes of music stored as MIDI messages takes about:
why: 3 minutes in about 3 kB, versus WAV storing 1 minute in about 10 MB.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: How many MIDI channels are there?
why: 16 channels, numbered 0-15, carried in the low 4 bits of the status byte.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The MIDI channel number occupies which bits of the status byte?
why: The channel is the last four (least significant) bits.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In General MIDI, channel 10 is reserved for:
why: Channel 10 is reserved for percussion instruments (drums).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Messages that carry no channel number and address all instruments are:
why: System messages, e.g. a change in tuning or timing, go to all instruments.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: A MIDI keyboard on its own:
why: It generates MIDI messages; it may also include a synthesizer.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Timbre is:
choices: The loudness envelope of a note
why: Timbre is what instrument is emulated, e.g. piano vs violin: the quality of the sound.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: '16-part multi-timbral' means a module can play:
why: Multi-timbral = different instrument sounds at once; polyphony counts simultaneous notes.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: '64 voices of polyphony' means a module can play:
why: Polyphony is the number of voices (notes) produced at the same time.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In MIDI, a 'voice' is:
choices: Each timbre and pitch at once
A system message sent to all channels
why: Every different timbre and pitch the tone module can produce at the same time.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The set of control settings that defines a particular timbre is a:
why: A patch defines a timbre; patches are organised into databases called banks.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: General MIDI defines how many patches for standard instruments?
why: 128 patches; plus a percussion map of 47 sounds.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: A General MIDI device must have at least how many dynamically allocated voices?
why: It must support all 16 channels, be multi-timbral and polyphonic, and have at least 24 voices.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: A MIDI status byte has a value between:
why: Status bytes have MSB = 1 (128-255); data bytes have MSB = 0 (0-127).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: How many bits does one MIDI byte occupy on the wire?
why: 8 data bits plus a 0 start bit and a stop bit.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Status byte 0x93 means:
why: High nibble 9 = Note On (&H9n); low nibble n = 3.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Status byte 0xC5 is:
why: &HCn = program change; n = 5. Control change is &HBn, pitch bend &HEn.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Note On for the drum channel (channel 10 counted from 1) has status byte:
why: Channels are numbered 0-15 in the byte, so channel 10 is n = 9: 0x99.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The MIDI serial connection runs at:
why: A 31.25 kbps serial link with 10-bit bytes.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: MIDI communication is:
why: The slide states MIDI communication is half-duplex.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The MIDI THRU port:
why: THRU simply copies data entering the IN channel, for daisy-chaining.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: One 3-byte MIDI note message takes about:
why: 30 bits / 31 250 bit/s = 0.00096 s. (0.77 ms wrongly uses 8-bit bytes.)

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Ten Note On plus ten Note Off messages take about:

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Recording one sound through several bandpass filters and mapping each to keys is:
why: Multisampling makes pitch shifting more reliable, since less shift is needed per note.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Quantization and transformation of data together are known as:
why: Quantization and transformation are collectively known as coding of the data.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The three stages of every compression scheme, in order, are:
why: 1 transformation, 2 loss (quantization), 3 coding (codewords).

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: The main lossy step in a compression scheme is:
why: Quantization uses fewer reconstruction levels than the original, so information is lost.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: Huffman coding belongs to which compression stage?
why: The coding stage assigns codewords, fixed- or variable-length such as Huffman.

chapter: L3 · SNR, Filtering, MIDI & Audio Coding
q: In the PCM decoder chain, what follows the µ-law/A-law expander?
why: Figure 6.15: DAC → expander → low-pass filter → output analog speech.
